title: Question 13
stem:
Copper-66 is a radioactive isotope.
When a nucleus of copper-66 decays, the emissions include a $\beta^-$ particle and a $\gamma$-ray photon.
The count rate produced from a sample of the isotope copper-66 is measured using a detector and counter, as illustrated in Fig. 13.1.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State three reasons why the activity of the sample of copper-66 is not equal to the measured count rate.

markscheme_points.text: e.g. background count (rate)/radiation multiple possible counts from each decay radiation emitted in all directions dead-time of counter (daughter) product unstable/also emits radiation self-absorption of radiation in sample or absorption in air/detector window three sensible suggestions, 1 each

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
In a time of $42.0\text{ minutes}$, the count rate from the sample of copper-66 is found to decrease from $3.62 \times 10^{4}\text{ Bq}$ to $1.21 \times 10^{2}\text{ Bq}$.
Calculate the half-life of copper-66.

$\text{half-life} = \text{..................................................... minutes}$
hints: Hint 1: Identify all given parameters and units, then recall the fundamental equation in nuclear physics and radioactive decay connecting them.
Hint 2: Rearrange the algebraic equation to isolate the target variable before substituting numerical values.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Identify Governing Principle**
State the core physical principle governing this problem: Nuclear physics and radioactive decay. Identify the relationship between the given quantities.

Step 2: **Substitute Values & Calculate**
Work through the substitution and calculation systematically:
A = A0 exp(- ln 2 × t / T½) 1.21 × 102 = 3.62 × 104 exp(- ln2 × 42.0 / T½) or 1.21 × 102 = 3.62 × 104 exp(-λ × 42.0); T½ = 5.1 minutes (306 s)
Verify intermediate arithmetic carefully.

Step 3: **Units & Significant Figures**
State the final result clearly with appropriate significant figures (typically 2 or 3 s.f.) and standard SI units.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The $\gamma$-ray photons emitted from radioactive nuclei have specific energies, dependent on the nucleus emitting the photons.
By comparison with emission line spectra, suggest what can be deduced about energy levels in nuclei.
